method: node --expose-gc scripts/probe-atlas-perf-baseline.mjs — median of 5 forced-GC rounds
why: Wall-clock is machine-relative and is never gated. Allocation per operation is a property of
the code rather than the host, so it is the axis that can be enforced across CI and dev machines.
Ceilings are set only on the PER-FRAME paths, where allocation churn is what produces hitches
and where the measurement is most stable (the three verification runs agreed exactly on all
A ceiling carries headroom above the measured value so a normal recompile does not flake it.
Headroom is NOT a target: 'measuredBytesPerOp' is the number to compare against when judging a
change, and raising a ceiling to make a regression pass requires a recorded justification.

interaction/pickMapTargetAt@500.why: Runs on every pointer move over the map. It allocates nothing today and must keep allocating nothing — this is the input-to-highlight critical path.

lane/projectOntoLane.why: Called per tick while the travel drive is engaged (travelLanes.update -> resolveLaneSegment -> projectOntoLane). The 72 B is the returned {alongWU, offAxisWU} object, not hidden churn, but design/PERF_BUDGET.md forbids per-frame allocation on hot paths — see the P3 finding filed against this. The ceiling pins it from growing while that is adjudicated.

lane/resolveLaneSegment.why: The per-tick lane fix, called directly from travelLanes.update (line 197). Includes projectOntoLane's allocation. Same doctrine tension as above.

markerLayout/layoutMapLabels@400.why: The declutter/collision pass. Not per-frame today (it runs on map model rebuild), so the ceiling is generous and exists to catch a step change in the algorithm rather than to enforce a tight budget. Its WALL-CLOCK cost is the more interesting number and is recorded, not gated — see the P2 finding on superlinear growth.
